newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr hits 10-mth low on yen,data eclipsed.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr hits 10-mth low on yen,data eclipsed.

text.p: The Australian dollar egded lower at the midsession as a booming yen drowned out the positive tone from upbeat domestic housing data.

Traders reported heavy Tokyo selling of AUD/yen after US$/yen slumped below 112.00 in a stop loss rout to 111.40. The local currency lost 3/4 yen in a matter of minutes to touch its lowest level since August last year. The pressure spilled over in AUD/US$, although support at US$0.7585 provided a cushion.
Data showing a healthy 12.2 percent rise in April mortgage commitments was lost in all the noise, but did at least confirm the vital housing sector was well on the way to recovery.
By 12.15 pm (0215 GMT) the local currency was holding the line at US$0.7590/95 having backtracked from a US$0.7628 high overnight and US$0.7610/15 late here Tuesday.
On the crosses it fled to 84.32/42 yen from an early 85.10/20 and 85.95/05 late Tuesday.
It was hot on the heels of the U.S. dollar which at one point slid below 111.00 yen for the first time since November last year having lost more than a yen since the opening.
Traders attributed much of the fall to panic stop loss selling but added it reflected underlying unease about Japan's trade surplus which was growing again after months of decline.

Data for April out this morning showed Japan's current account surplus had ballooned by 92.7 percent on the same month last year to 1.09 trillion yen. That implied an increased net demand for yen for trade purposes and also stirred concerns of renewed trade friction between Japan and the U.S.
Those worries were stoked by comments from U.S. deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers that Japan should avoid running up external surpluses that would hurt global growth.
Analysts said the market suspected Japan was keen to see a higher yen short term to deflect any trade criticism that might be levelled at the forthcoming G7 meeting in Denver.

The latest slide in AUD/yen brought the local currency's losses to more than 15 percent since it peaked at 100.00 yen on May 1. And there was little in the way of chart support to prevent it from plumbing the 82.00 trough touched in early August last year.

That was a bleak picture for Japanese investors who had bought A$ denominated debt, particularly those dual currency samurais with a currency option -- largely US$ and A$ -- which became popular in March and April. Analysts said speculation was the Japanese securities houses which issued these were sitting on total losses of more than 100 billion yen.

Such a painful experience would have curbed Japanese demand for A$ debt even if the Reserve Bank had not cut interest rates last month, but the sharp fall in A$ yields since would not haved helped either.

The dollar's attraction was further dimmed by persistent speculation the RBA would yet ease again, and endless talk in Japan about the likely timing of a Bank of Japan tightening. The latter may actually be a little clearer once the next quarterly Tankan report is released on June 25.
For domestic policy, jobs data on Thursday could have the market slavering for another cut despite today's housing news.
The 12.2 percent rise in housing finance was the largest monthly gain since late 1993 and took total commitments to their highest level since July 1994.
Lending for new construction rose 12.1 percent to be 14.5 percent up on the year, which promised to fuelling growth in the housing and building sectors this year.

However, those looking for another easing could argue a housing recovery was always expected and the RBA was more concerned with taking advantage of subdued inflation to reduce stubbornly high levels of unemployment.
